summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that the offence covers sodomy and acts involving contact between males that a reasonable person would regard as indecent. Sodomy is classified in the Criminal Code as unlawful sexual conduct, defined as anal sexual intercourse or any indecent act between consenting adults, with common-law formulations reaching "unlawful and intentional sexual relations per anum between two human males" and "unnatural offences".

A 2006 revision of the Criminal Code expanded sodomy beyond sexual activity to any act involving contact between two males that a reasonable person would regard as an indecent act, and added a sexual deviancy offence criminalising holding hands, hugging or kissing between two people of the same sex. That amendment was one of fifteen additions made to the code that year. Conduct well short of intercourse therefore falls inside the criminal law, and visible affection between two people read as of the same sex is exposed to it.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024) examines escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people across the countries it covers, Zimbabwe among them. The deployment of law as an instrument of hostility is the risk context a visitor faces, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Zimbabwean law provides no general protection from discrimination, violence or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only explicit protections tied to sexual orientation concern personal information, under the Freedom of Information Act (2020) and the Cyber and Data Protection Act (2022).

The Constitution was amended in 2013 to define marriage as between a man and a woman, and in May 2019 Cabinet approved amendments to the marriage law to align the ban. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition of that partnership and no protection attaching to it.

Gender marker change is not permitted. Section 18(2) of the Births and Deaths Registration Act allows a first-name change only by application to the Registrar General with evidence justifying the need, and the Registrar General's discretion can defeat a change sought on grounds of gender identity.

Enforcement has a documented record. In 2014 the activist Rikki Nathanson was arrested for using a women's bathroom under a criminal nuisance charge; the charge was dismissed and she sued for damages and won. In 1998 former President Canaan Banana was convicted on eleven charges of sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault following his 1996 arrest, sentenced to ten years' imprisonment, and released after serving six months in an open prison.

Government campaigns against homosexual men and women have run since 1995. Documented enforcement includes infiltration of GALZ, bribery, detention, beating, killing and rape by authorities, and the reported use of the Central Intelligence Organisation to beat and arrest homosexuals.

Healthcare is the clearest area of formal protection. In July 2018 the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that providing care to these groups is lawful and every provider's duty, recording that "nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups", and it was issued because patients had been avoiding clinics out of fear of mistreatment or of staff tipping off the police. Health ministry training manuals further require professionals to support the specific healthcare needs of transgender and non-gender-conforming people, alongside sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject drugs.

Reachable support infrastructure is thin but present. GALZ, established in 1990, reports more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, and offers legal support covering arrests for sodomy, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes.
tangentialFactors:
Section 11 of the Censorship and Entertainments Control Act prohibits undesirable publications, defined as indecent or obscene or offensive or harmful to public morals or likely to be contrary to public health. That provision has been used to harass LGBTQ people and activists, an expression and materials exposure that sits alongside the person-level criminal law.

The Amnesty International report of 9 January 2024 places Zimbabwe within a set of African countries where law is being turned against LGBTI populations, so travel within the region does not by itself lower the exposure described here.
localsOnly:
Transgender Zimbabweans face difficulty accessing legal work because official documents do not reflect their gender, as documented in comments attributed to the activist Jordan Chanetsa, who also cites the documents problem as a barrier beyond employment.

Rikki Nathanson established Trans Research, Education, Advocacy & Training (TREAT) in 2015, the year after her arrest and the civil claim that followed it.

The 2018 health ministry handbook records the domestic public-health position: criminalisation of sex work, drug use and some sexual acts creates disproportionate harms, undermines HIV prevention for the whole nation, and impairs access to healthcare.
outOfScopeNotes:
How often the sodomy and sexual deviancy provisions have been charged in recent years is not established in the available sources. No charge-level figures were located, so the distance between the statute as written and its day-to-day application remains unresolved.

The text of the 2006 amendment was not obtained directly. The scope of the sexual deviancy offence and the examples attached to it rest on reference material and contemporaneous reporting.

Whether health providers in public institutions follow the 2018 handbook in practice, and whether the police tip-offs the handbook was designed to prevent continue, is not documented. Day-to-day treatment of trans patients therefore depends on staff trained under that handbook.

The May 2019 Cabinet approval of marriage-law amendments is recorded as an approval; whether those amendments were enacted, and in what final form, is not sourced.
